set.hook: Raquel Carena's Belleville blackboard since 1987: offal, braises and a natural-wine cellar
set.why: Raquel Carena came from Argentina with no kitchen training and has cooked at this Belleville address since 1987; her partner Philippe 'Pinuche' Pinoteau took over the bottles in 1992, when few Paris cellars bothered with natural wine. Pierre Hermé told Purepeople in December 2025 that he has been eating here for nearly 30 years, and Time Out says he still comes at least every two weeks. In 2026 Isabelle Huppert named it her favourite Paris bistro.

set.hook: Saint-Germain's 1880 Alsatian brasserie: choucroute, sole meunière, a listed 1900 dining room
set.why: Léonard Lipp, an Alsatian, opened a beer hall here on 27 October 1880 and served cervelat rémoulade; after 1920 Marcellin Cazes made it a literary address and founded the Prix Cazes, still awarded each November with a table at Lipp as part of the prize. set.hook: The 1896 broth hall on Faubourg Montmartre: shared tables, the bill written on the paper cloth
set.why: Frédéric and Camille Chartier opened it in 1896 as a bouillon, a cheap meat-and-broth canteen for working Paris, and the hall with its globe lamps was classé monument historique in 1989. The Joulie family bought it in 2007 and has since put the name on further rooms at Montparnasse and Gare de l'Est. The flagship still takes no bookings, serves without a break from late morning to midnight, and the waiter adds up your bill in pen on the tablecloth.

set.hook: Bertrand Larcher's Marais crêperie: Bordier butter, Breton buckwheat and a long cider list
set.why: Bertrand Larcher opened his first Breizh Café in Tokyo in the mid-1990s, then one in Cancale, and in 2007, per Mes Prestiges, this one on rue Vieille du Temple. The Japanese years show in the sourcing: Jean-Yves Bordier butter, IGP Breton buckwheat, Cancale oysters, and a cider list read like a wine card. The wood-panelled room serves all day, and Frommer's warns it fills up, so book.

set.hook: A rue du Montparnasse crêperie for lace-edged buckwheat and cider served in a bowl
set.why: Gare Montparnasse was the Paris end of the line from Brittany, and Bretons who came for work settled around it; rue du Montparnasse still has a crêperie every few doors. Josselin, at number 67, is the one Time Out singles out for its queue, even on weekdays, and generous fillings at rarely more than EUR 20 a head. Do not mix it up with Le Petit Josselin, a separate house at number 59.

set.hook: Steak-frites without a menu: walnut salad, contrefilet, a secret sauce, then a second helping
set.why: Paul Gineste de Saurs opened the original in 1959, and two houses now descend from it: the Relais de Venise near Porte Maillot, and this one, Marie-Paule Burrus's Relais de l'Entrecôte, with rooms on rue Saint-Benoît, rue Marbeuf and boulevard du Montparnasse and branches abroad, Dubai among them. The only question asked is how you want the meat cooked. The herb-butter sauce has never been published, and the steak arrives in two servings so the second is still hot.

wine.title: The cellar comes first
wine.story: In these rooms the wine list was there before the menu and the person who runs it owns the place. At Le Baratin in Belleville, Philippe Pinoteau has poured natural wine since 1992 beside Raquel Carena, who has cooked there since 1987. At Parcelles, in a 1936 café on rue Chapon, sommelier Bastien Fidelin also runs the wine shop across the street, and Gault&Millau's 2026 review scores the kitchen 13/20. At Vantre on rue de la Fontaine-au-Roi, Marco Pelletier, formerly of Le Bristol and Taillevent, won a Wine Spectator Grand Award in 2019 for a room of about 30 seats, open weekdays only.
wine.where: Le Baratin on rue Jouye-Rouve; Parcelles on rue Chapon; Vantre on rue de la Fontaine-au-Roi

brasserie.title: Alsace came to Paris
brasserie.story: The Paris brasserie began as a beer hall, often Alsatian, and these three still serve choucroute under listed ceilings. Bofinger near the Bastille dates from 1864 and its glass-domed room was open for Heritage Days tours in 2026. Brasserie Lipp opened on boulevard Saint-Germain in 1880 and hands out its own literary award, the Prix Cazes, every November; Gault&Millau's 2026 review finds its carte barely changed since the 1950s. La Coupole arrived in Montparnasse in 1927 with pillars painted by 27 artists and a lamb curry that has never left the menu. Groupe Bertrand now owns all three.
brasserie.where: Bofinger on rue de la Bastille; Brasserie Lipp on boulevard Saint-Germain; La Coupole on boulevard du Montparnasse

bouillon.title: Cheap since the 1800s
bouillon.story: Bouillons were invented in the 1850s by Pierre-Louis Duval, a butcher, to feed the workers of Les Halles broth and boiled beef for very little money. Bouillon Chartier on rue du Faubourg Montmartre has done it since 1896, in a hall listed in 1989, with no bookings and waiters who write the bill on the tablecloth. Bouillon Pigalle revived the format in 2017 with 300 seats; Gault&Millau's 2026 review prices its bourguignon at EUR 12.20. Polidor started as a crémerie in 1845 and has a different plat du jour for every weekday, the semainier.
bouillon.where: Bouillon Chartier on rue du Faubourg Montmartre; Bouillon Pigalle on boulevard de Clichy; Polidor on rue Monsieur-le-Prince

day.title: No booking, or book weeks out
day.story: Two rooms in the 11th that run on daytime hours and work in opposite ways. Clamato on rue de Charonne, opened in 2013 by the Septime team, has never taken a reservation: you queue, and the menu depends on what the boats from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, Concarneau and the Île d'Yeu sent that morning. MICHELIN gives it a Bib Gourmand. Mokonuts on rue Saint-Bernard, near the Aligre market, has about twenty seats, serves weekdays only and closes in the afternoon; tables go weeks ahead, and Paris by Mouth's 2026 revisit kept it on its favourites list. If you cannot get a table, buy the cookies.
day.where: Clamato on rue de Charonne; Mokonuts on rue Saint-Bernard

window.title: Lunch eaten standing up
window.story: Paris street lunch is eaten standing up, and the queue is part of the meal. L'As du Fallafel has served pita from its green window on rue des Rosiers since 1979; it is kosher, so it shuts at 17:00 on Friday and stays closed Saturday. Chez Alain Miam Miam made its name at a stall in the Marché des Enfants Rouges, which fire destroyed in October 2026; its own counter on rue Charlot builds toasted sandwiches by hand, but check it is open. Le Petit Vendôme on rue des Capucines sells ham and butter on a baguette, ranked the world's best sandwich by Time Out in 2025.
window.where: L'As du Fallafel on rue des Rosiers; Chez Alain Miam Miam on rue Charlot; Le Petit Vendôme on rue des Capucines

onedish.title: One dish, done the same way
onedish.story: Each of these rooms serves one main dish and has kept it the same for decades. Bretons came to Paris through Gare Montparnasse, and La Crêperie de Josselin on rue du Montparnasse makes buckwheat galettes on a billig and pours cider into bowls. Breizh Café in the Marais, founded by Bertrand Larcher after he opened in Tokyo, makes the same galette with Bordier butter and IGP buckwheat. Le Relais de l'Entrecôte on rue Saint-Benoît has offered one menu since 1959: walnut salad, then steak-frites in a sauce whose recipe has never been published, with the second helping included.
onedish.where: La Crêperie de Josselin on rue du Montparnasse; Breizh Café on rue Vieille du Temple; Le Relais de l'Entrecôte on rue Saint-Benoît
